newsitem.title: USA: Former broker settles insider trading charges.
newsitem.headline: Former broker settles insider trading charges.

text.p: A former broker for Merrill Lynch agreed to pay penalities to settle civil charges he violated securities laws by helping others trade on confidential information, regulators said Tuesday.

Without admitting or denying the allegations, Michael Sweeney, 50, a registered representative with Merrill Lynch Pierce Fenner & Smith Inc. from 1983 through 1993, agreed to pay $25,000 to the U.S. Treasury, the commission said.

Sweeney also was barred from association with any broker, dealer, investment adviser, investment company or municipal securities dealer. The commission ordered him to cease and desist from committing any future violations of federal laws.
Attempts to reach Sweeney's attorneys in New York City were unsuccessful.
In an administrative proceeding, SEC alleged Sweeney aided and abetted a group of investors engaged in an insider trading scheme involving AT&T Corp. takeover targets.

The SEC alleged from at least 1989 through 1991, Sweeney advised Charles Brumfield and Thomas Alger, then employees of AT&T, on how to use the information to trade in three of the companies AT&T sought to acquire -- NCR Corp., Digital Microwave Corp. and Teradata Corp.
Sweeney allegedly counseled them to trade through the brokerage accounts of other persons in an effort to avoid detection, the commission said.
In addition to providing advice, Sweeney allegedly facilitated illegal trading by passing confidential information and trading instructions from Alger to Robert Flanagan, a friend, SEC said.
Merrill Lynch fired Sweeney after he refused to cooperate in an internal investigation it conducted, SEC said.

In October 1996, Brumfield, former labor relations vice president in AT&T's human resources department was sentenced to four years probation, six months in a community treatment center and fined $6,000.
Alger, Brumfield's friend and subordinate in the human resources department, was sentenced in August 1996 to three years probation, 300 hours of community service and fined $1,000, SEC said.
Flanagan, a mutual friend of Alger and Sweeney, was sentenced in August 1996 to 24 months in prison, three years supervised release and fined $5,000.

The overall scheme, which extended from December 1988 to about 1993, is believed to have netted 18 participants about $2.6 million in illegal profits involving four targets: NCR Corp., Paradyne Corp., Digitial and Teradata. None of the companies is now owned by AT&T.
